title: Multiply Strings
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated string addition versus direct digit-by-digit multiplication with positional carries.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two non negative integers num1 and num2, represented as strings, return their product, also as a string, without converting either input directly into a single large built in integer.

blocks.text: Given two non negative integers num1 and num2, represented as strings, return their product, also as a string, without converting either input directly into a single large built in integer.

blocks.title: Analogy: Multiplication the Way It Is Taught on Paper
blocks.text: This is exactly the multiplication method taught in school, multiplying every digit of one number by every digit of the other, writing each partial product one column over from the last, and adding everything up column by column at the end. Doing it this way never requires holding either full number as one giant value at once.

blocks.caption: Multiply every pair of digits, then place and combine the results by position

blocks.text: Multiplying by zero always gives "0", regardless of how large the other number is.
This problem sits right next to Add Binary in the sheet, and it is worth checking exactly how far reusing that string addition idea gets you, and where it genuinely stops being enough.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This problem forbids converting to a native big integer, echoing the exact same constraint as Add Binary, only now the operation is multiplication instead of addition.

Observation 2: A tempting reuse of Add Binary's own string addition helper is to add num1 to a running total, once for every unit in num2's value, and this is genuinely correct.

Observation 3: The problem is that this cost scales with the numeric VALUE num2 represents, not its digit count, and value grows exponentially with digit count, so a num2 with just a few more digits explodes the number of additions needed, a danger a small test case like 12 times 3 completely hides.

Observation 4: Grade school long multiplication avoids this entirely by multiplying every individual pair of digits directly, and since a digit at position i in num1 and a digit at position j in num2 always contribute to exactly the same two positions, i plus j and i plus j plus 1, in the result, regardless of any other digit pair, every partial product can be placed directly into a shared result array instead of computed and added as a whole separate number each time.

That distinction, cost proportional to a value versus cost proportional to a digit count, is exactly what separates an approach that looks fine on small examples from one that is genuinely fast for any input this problem allows.
Treat num2 as a count, and add num1 to a running total that many times, using string addition, similar to the technique from Add Binary, generalized to base 10.

items: If either input is "0", return "0" immediately.
Parse num2 into an ordinary number to use as a count.
Start a running total at "0".
Add num1 to the running total, using string addition, once for every count.
Return the final running total.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: repeatedly add num1 to a running total, num2 times

blocks.text: This is correct, since repeatedly adding num1 exactly as many times as the value of num2 is precisely what multiplication means.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(value of num2 times n), where n is the length of num1. Since the value of an m digit number can be as large as almost 10 to the power of m, this is exponential in the number of digits of num2, not just proportional to its length.
Space: O(n plus m), for the running total as it grows.

Limitation: the number of additions needed grows explosively with just a few more digits in num2, since the VALUE of a number grows exponentially with its digit count. Multiplying digit by digit directly, the same way multiplication is done on paper, needs only as many individual digit multiplications as there are pairs of digits, not one operation per unit of value.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why repeated addition works but is wasteful: it performs one full string addition per unit of num2's value, and that value can be exponentially larger than num2's digit count would suggest.

What stays the same as Add Binary: the underlying discipline of never assuming a native integer type is wide enough, working with the digits directly instead.

What is different here: instead of adding two numbers digit by digit, this problem multiplies two numbers, and each individual digit pair contributes to a fixed, predictable pair of positions in the final result.

Can every digit pair be handled completely independently: yes, a digit at position i in num1 and a digit at position j in num2 always land at positions i plus j and i plus j plus 1 in the result, regardless of any other digit pair, so every product can be added directly into a shared result array.

The core idea: multiply every pair of digits once, add each product into its two predictable result positions, letting values of 10 or more carry into the position just before, then read off the final digits.

Multiply every digit of num1 by every digit of num2 directly. A digit at position i in num1 and a digit at position j in num2, counting from the right, contributes to positions i plus j and i plus j plus 1 in the result. Add each product into its correct position, letting values of 10 or more carry into the position just before it, then read off the final digits.
Multiply every pair of digits directly, adding each product into its two predictable result positions and letting overflow carry into the position before it.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: multiply each pair of digits and place the product at its correct position

codes.python:
def multiply(num1, num2):
    if num1 == "0" or num2 == "0":
        return "0"                                   # multiplying by zero is always zero
    n, m = len(num1), len(num2)
    result = [0] * (n + m)                           # one slot for every possible digit position
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        for j in range(m - 1, -1, -1):
            mul = int(num1[i]) * int(num2[j])            # multiply this one pair of digits
            p1, p2 = i + j, i + j + 1                     # the two positions this product can affect
            total = mul + result[p2]
            result[p2] = total % 10                        # the digit that lands in this position
            result[p1] += total // 10                       # whatever carries into the next position
    digits = "".join(map(str, result)).lstrip("0")        # drop any leading zeroes
    return digits if digits else "0"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    num1, num2 = "123", "456"
    print(multiply(num1, num2))

blocks.text: This works because the value of digit at position i in num1 (from the right, weighted 10 to the i) times the digit at position j in num2 (weighted 10 to the j) always contributes exactly 10 to the power of i plus j to the true product, and any single digit product that reaches 10 or more simply needs its excess carried one position further left, exactly the position i plus j formula already accounts for. Since this holds independently for every one of the n times m digit pairs, accumulating all of them into one shared result array, with carries resolved along the way, reconstructs the exact same product long multiplication produces on paper.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m), a genuine complexity class improvement from exponential in the number of digits down to simply proportional to the number of digit pairs.
Space: O(n plus m), for the result array, this is the floor for this problem, since a product of that many digits must always be produced, and every pair of digits genuinely needs to be multiplied at least once.

blocks.text: This is the standard grade school multiplication algorithm, and its key insight is that a digit at position i and a digit at position j always combine at a fixed, predictable position in the result, letting every partial product be placed directly rather than computed and added separately. Very large number multiplication has even faster algorithms, such as Karatsuba multiplication, but those are well beyond what this problem or a typical interview setting expects.

blocks.text: This problem is explicitly designed to test digit by digit multiplication rather than relying on a built in big integer type, so proactively stating that constraint and why the position formula i plus j works is a strong way to show real understanding rather than just reciting a memorized solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "is repeated addition fast enough", think: no, its cost scales with num2's numeric value, which grows exponentially with its digit count, not with the digit count itself.
If the interviewer says "how do you know where a digit product lands", think: a digit at position i times a digit at position j always contributes to positions i plus j and i plus j plus 1.
If the interviewer says "how is this related to Add Binary", think: both avoid a native integer type by working digit by digit with explicit carries, just for a different operation.

How would you adapt this approach to also support negative numbers, given a separate sign for each input?
How would this problem change if the inputs were given in a base other than 10, like hexadecimal strings?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The repeated addition approach runs in time proportional to the actual value of num2, which grows exponentially with its digit count, using O(n plus m) space. The digit by digit multiplication approach runs in O(n times m) time, a genuine complexity class improvement, using the same O(n plus m) space for the result.

items: Pattern: digit by digit multiplication with positional carries, the grade school long multiplication algorithm applied directly to two digit strings.

Core Idea: a digit at position i in num1 times a digit at position j in num2 always contributes to exactly positions i plus j and i plus j plus 1 in the result, so every digit pair can be multiplied once and placed directly into a shared result array instead of relying on repeated addition scaled to a value that can be exponentially large.
Time: O(value of num2 times n) for the brute force, exponential in num2's digit count; O(n times m) for the optimized version.
Space: O(n plus m) for both versions.
Most Important Observation: an approach whose cost depends on a number's value rather than its digit count looks fine on small examples but is not truly efficient.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the repeated addition version; recognizing why it is not truly efficient, and deriving the fixed digit-position formula, is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: digit i times digit j lands at positions i plus j and i plus j plus 1, accumulate with carries, strip leading zeroes.
